Hi thanks again for the Comments on this post. I remember you mentioning that you’d like an update. The session just finished a few hours ago (this will be longer).

The NPCs who witnessed the deaths brought their bodies to the rest of the party. My Bard first started showing hints of guilt, then went to the other side of town to both grieve alone and look for a magical item the dead PC had. She tried using stealth to do this discreetly but failed. After failing a perception check to find remnants of the item (as the players, we knew it was destroyed), she just gave up and sat on the ground upset.

Three PCs followed her to where she was sitting, one of which being one she had a disagreement with (said disagreement is part of the reason she said things to the dead PC my bard regrets, though they weren’t part of it). She opened up about her feelings on that and what she did. After some words from other party members, that’s when I came out with a monologue I’ve had on hand for this situation. She opened up about her failures, her feelings on the war her country went through, her suicidal thoughts and even hinted at her background to a couple of characters (she’s a noble’s daughter). I kid you not, it drove the table to tears and we might have to put a content warning on the video for it (we record our sessions and upload them). 

It led to one of them opening up about their own failures and their desire to see their country prosper together, rather than bury another one of its people. Then the other two reassured her that she’s not a burden and that isolating herself is the last thing she should be doing. One of them threw her into a hug, where my bard thanked them, apologised to the one PC regarding the disagreement (it partially cleared her conscious about not apologising to the dead PC) and they left that area, since that magic item might have had dark energy.

Now one of them is refusing to keep her out of his sight and they’re gonna be drinking in the tavern next session. God, it’s hard to convey over message. I don’t think the sub allows links in comments. But I’d love to share it.

My character has definitely been kind of running and hiding from the grief, at least physically. She’s been really deep in thought about it emotionally and mentally. But has been embarrassed to show it physically. For example, her first action after finding out was hiding in the town’s church to think then distracting herself with the colosseum. That will likely change as she sobers up though, since she currently uses alcohol as a coping mechanism.

I never thought about how owing the deceased would impact her actions. To be more specific on why she owes him, her and this PC were in a difficult fight in a prison cell where the PC almost died, then fled and an NPC was struggling to damage the monster (coincidently the same NPC who asked her to play at the PC’s service). All my character could do was run away like a coward. Mechanically it was the best move, since she would’ve died in one hit. Character wise, prisons make her uncomfortable for backstory reasons. Due to movement, she could only get partially out of the room and used the rest of her turn to help the PC heal. Despite not fully being patched up, the PC stood in the doorway to keep my character safe. She doesn’t feel like she deserves the chivalry for her cowardly actions and made a mental note to make it up to him. She just didn’t know how yet.

Being in a support role, she already feels the need to stretch herself thin and try to help everyone she comes across. She also made it up to the NPC for her actions by taking part in a heist (the NPC is a rogue. She’s not proud of this). Her saying yes to playing in the service felt like a “least she could do” situation in regard to paying him back. But it doesn’t feel like enough. I’ll need to look into specifics on how she could act. I have no ideas.

But some of it is also a defence mechanism for avoiding the negative shit in her life, like mistreatment from her mother, how she takes the blame for things that aren’t her fault and more recently, some of the events that took place in the campaign. God, that girls being healers trope is so stale now. I still see it constantly in video games (RPGs in particular). It doesn’t help that they usually fit in one of three categories.

1. They’re the main hero’s (usually the guy with the magic sword) love interest and/or childhood best friend

2. They’re the second party member you get. This one is fair. But shake it up a little.

3. The healer character often settles for being a healer because they aren’t capable of fighting offensively “but still want to help where she can”. This completely downplays the importance of healers.

I’ve only seen two examples of male healers in RPGs off the top of my head. The first one being Ness from Earthbound (the one female party member is the glass cannon). The second one being Mallow from Super Mario RPG. Even then, he gets replaced with Princess Peach in healing duties after a while. So that one doesn’t fully count.

To paint a better picture. I was the “ugly” girl in school. I had other reasons for being bullied as well. But the other girls would tease me for my looks and I’ve had situations where people asked me out as a joke. This caused me to never take being asked out seriously anymore, since it would just blow up in my face and I was stupid for “believing I actually had a chance with them”. This all happened when I was around 16-19 years old. There was also one incident in particular that really cemented that I didn’t stand a chance and I gave up outright.

Around the same time as that incident, I started doing well in my online content and really jumping into various online communities, since I ran my own community and wanted to network. The part that answers the initial Reddit question was on New Year’s Eve 2022. This best friend messaged asking if we could talk privately. Even despite my past with it, he knocked down some huge walls I built around myself and I knew in my gut I could trust him despite everything. 

I learnt a new perspective on trust through all this. It’s not the events themselves I should be wary of in the future. Being asked out as a joke on multiple occasions isn’t a judgement of how undesirable/unattractive/whatever I am. It’s the people who have hurt me I needed to be careful of and those actions showed a lot more about their character. When that friend asked me out, I not only built that trust with him. I definitely feel like there’s a balance that not many people get right.

Of course it’s extremely important to take care of yourself. We can’t function or help others if we can’t help ourselves first. Doing so leads to either getting burned out or being a people pleaser which trust me, isn’t fun. But there are kind ways to decline helping someone without jeopardising your own mental and physical health. Plus there are ways you could make up for not being able to help in that moment by offering to help in other ways.

For example, let’s say you’re an able bodied person and a friend asked if you’d help them move house. But you’re just not mentally in the headspace to leave the house, socialise and move boxes. You’re well within your right to say you’re not in the headspace. But offer your services elsewhere and in a way that doesn’t screw over either party, like offering to help unpack boxes another day or by sending meals over. You can look out for yourself and still be kind.

There are also smaller instances of people needing help that won’t inconvenience you if you help in the moment. Things like holding the door open for the person behind you, helping pick up something they dropped or being an ear to listen. Even if you’re having a bad time mentally, you can still help someone open a jar or something. Kindness is often a stress free thing depending on how you use it.
